How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • Industry observers note that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • It has been revealed that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly key sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

Industry observers note that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

It has been revealed that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly key sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Recent findings suggest that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this newly introduced phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

According to recent reports, these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

According to recent reports, performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve indicates the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

Industry observers note that when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

In a recent development, the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

In a recent development, the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Sources indicate that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

It has been revealed that builders using the new AWS experience on the Paid blueprint can now receive spend limit alerts by text message (SMS), alongside existing email notifications. A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost for a project. Notifications are sent as a project approaches its limit, and when a project reaches its limit, AWS automatically pauses it. SMS gives builders a second way to stay informed about their project costs.

Email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused. SMS alerts close this gap with a text message when a project's actual costs reach 90% of its spend limit, so builders have time to act, such as raising the limit or stopping resources they don't need.

It has been revealed that to turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits. Text alerts are only sent to verified numbers, and you can opt out at any time. SMS alerts for spend limits are available at no additional charge for US phone numbers, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa.

To learn more, see Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, the AWS Account Management Reference Guide, or Get started with AWS.

#34192. Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2328 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Sources indicate that when an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sr. Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Sources indicate that when an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback. Is it the code, the data, or the environment? Hard to say, as clues are scattered across task logs, scheduler logs, and worker metrics. And once you know what the problem is, the question becomes whether to add memory, rewrite the DAG, or finally take on the major version upgrade you've been putting off. Answering these questions takes time and deep Airflow expertise, usually while you're on call in the middle of an incident.

It has been revealed that AI agents can increasingly do much of this legwork. Managed Service for Apache Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) now offers agentic help across a pipeline's entire lifecycle. In the Google Cloud console, Managed Airflow Agent investigates failed tasks, recommends improvements to your environment, and checks whether your DAGs are ready for a newer Airflow version. In your IDE or coding agent, Data Agent Kit writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. In this post, we take you on a tour of these features through a story of a fictional company, Cymbal Shops.

Amira is a data engineer at Cymbal Shops, an online retailer running cymbal-prod, a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs, 4 GB of memory, and that autoscale between 1 and 6. Every click, search, and add-to-cart on Cymbal's website and mobile app goes to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Storage subscription writes the events as newline-delimited JSON files into hourly folders under gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/. It writes files in parallel and starts new ones every 5 minutes or every 128 MB, whichever comes first.

Analysts, meanwhile, want these events in BigQuery, cleaned and with personal data hashed — and they want them fast. Ideally, each file would be processed the moment it lands. But Cymbal's Airflow environment runs Airflow 2.11.1, and Airflow 2 has no native way to start a DAG run when something happens outside Airflow. You can get close: Schedule a DAG every few minutes and let a sensor wait for latest files, or build an extra service that triggers runs through the Airflow REST API. However, the team doesn't want all those moving parts, so they settle for the next best thing: an hourly batch.

In a recent development, amira writes her DAGs with an agent. She works in Antigravity with the Data Agent Kit plugin, which adds Google Data Cloud skills and tools to the agent, and she uses Gemini as her model. Setup takes a few minutes: She installs the plugin, signs in with her Google account, and selects her project and region.

In the agent panel, she describes what she needs with this prompt:.

"Write a DAG named clickstream_hourly for the Managed Airflow environment cymbal-prod in us-central1. Every hour, load the previous hour of clickstream events into the BigQuery table clickstream.events. The events are newline-delimited JSON files in gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/YYYY-MM-DD/HH/. Transform them with pandas: read each file into a DataFrame with the nested context object kept as a JSON string, combine the files with pd.concat, then drop malformed records, deduplicate on event_id (Pub/Sub delivers at least once), and hash user_email and ip_address. Re-running an hour must not create duplicates. If a run fails, email data-oncall@example.com. Validate the DAG and deploy it.".

Data Agent Kit inspects the target Managed Airflow environment in Antigravity, generates an Airflow 2.11-compatible DAG, and deploys it.

The agent checks the target environment before it writes any code. Because cymbal-prod runs Airflow 2.11.1, the agent produces the code aligned to that version. It then deploys the DAG to cymbal-prod and confirms that Airflow loads it without errors.

It has been revealed that amira reviews the code, and the DAG goes live in early August. It's good code: readable, idempotent, and correct for Airflow 2.11. A busy hour sees about 200 files and 350 MB, and the task peaks below 2 GB — well under the 4 GB worker limit.

Recent findings suggest that look at how the task builds its input, though. It lists every file in the hour's folder, reads each one into a DataFrame, and then pd.concat combines them into a single DataFrame. The unit of work is a clock hour, so the task needs more memory as traffic grows. That's fine until traffic changes...

The hourly task loads every JSON file from the previous hour into memory and combines them into a single DataFrame with pd.concat.

Sources indicate that late October brings two changes in the same week. Cymbal launches its "Fall Into Savings" campaign, and a fresh mobile app release adds much more detailed event tracking. Events from the new app version are about three times larger than their predecessors, and the campaign brings more traffic on top, so an hour of clicks grows from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB. Holding a whole hour in pandas takes several times its raw size, so load_previous_hour_clickstream now needs more memory than a worker’s allotted 4 GB. Autoscaling doesn't help here: It adds workers when tasks queue up, but each task still runs on a single worker and can't use more memory than that worker has.

On October 23, the 14:00 UTC run of clickstream_hourly fails. All three attempts die the same way, with no error in the task log.

Amira opens cymbal-prod in the console, where Managed Airflow Agent is built in. It diagnoses the problem and recommends a fix; Amira decides what to change.

She goes to the DAGs tab, selects clickstream_hourly, and opens Run history. Next to the failed 14:00 run there's an Investigate button with a sparkle icon. She clicks it, and a short ‘Investigate DAG run failure’ dialog asks her to confirm her choice. The Ask agent panel then opens next to the page, and the agent starts investigating.

Managed Airflow Agent investigates the failed run in the console, correlates worker memory metrics with task retries, and recommends fixes.

At the end of the report, the agent recommends three fixes: load the files straight into BigQuery, process them in batches, or give the workers more memory.

Look at what the agent delivers! Every conclusion includes the evidence that led to it, so Amira can check the reasoning herself.

According to recent reports, two of the recommendations are code changes, and code changes take time to write and test. With every hourly run now failing, Amira needs the quick fix first: more memory for the workers. But how much? The right number depends on the whole environment, not on one task. So she asks the agent in the same panel:.

"clickstream_hourly runs out of memory on 4 GB workers. Analyze the cymbal-prod environment and recommend how much worker memory it needs, along with any other improvements.".

Managed Airflow Agent analyzes environment-wide telemetry, recommends 8 GB worker memory, and flags resilience and retention gaps.

The agent recommends increasing worker memory from 4 GB to 8 GB, and flags three production-readiness gaps: Database retention is disabled, the environment isn't highly resilient, and it has no scheduled snapshots.

In a recent development, amira acts on the first recommendation right away. The agent is read-only, so she makes the change herself and increases worker memory to 8 GB.

In a recent development, she schedules the other two recommendations for the next change window. With 8 GB workers, the pipeline gets through the rest of the campaign.

It has been revealed that but that only buys time. Black Friday traffic is forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, and at that volume the hourly batch will need well over 8 GB. The troubleshooting report had already named the real problem: a unit of work that grows with traffic. That brings Amira back to what the team wanted in the first place, which was to process each file as soon as it lands.

Sources indicate that airflow 3 makes that much easier, because it supports event-driven scheduling natively. An asset watcher listens to an external source, such as a Pub/Sub subscription. When upcoming messages arrive, it updates an asset, and any DAG scheduled on that asset starts a run. Under the hood, the watcher still checks the subscription every few seconds, but it does so inside Airflow's triggerer. No DAG needs to be scheduled just so a sensor can wait for files, and no extra service has to trigger runs. Each run gets the new messages in its payload, so it can work on just the files that landed, one task per file, and memory per task depends on file size, not on how busy the hour is.

Sources indicate that A major version upgrade of a production environment isn't something to do blind. Before anyone touches the code, Amira asks the agent in the same panel:.

"Check whether cymbal-prod is ready to upgrade to Airflow 3.".

Managed Airflow Agent can also check upgrade readiness. It checks compatibility of the environment's DAGs with a given version. Amira is checking what problems she might have while migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3). The agent reports the following observations:.

Managed Airflow Agent scans DAGs in cymbal-prod for Airflow 3 compatibility blockers before migration.

Two findings are blockers. The first comes as a surprise: a maintenance DAG that cleans up the Airflow database by hand, which Airflow 3 no longer allows. The agent's fix is to retire it and turn on database retention, the same feature it recommended during the incident. The second, marketing_attribution, still uses execution_date, which Airflow 3 removed. Four DAGs also need schedule_interval renamed to schedule.

Sources indicate that in a few minutes, the agent estimated the work to be done. To perform the upgrade, the report suggests using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill.

Rather than upgrading in place, Amira creates a new Airflow 3 environment alongside cymbal-prod to move the DAGs there.

Back in Antigravity, Data Agent Kit's migrations skill takes over. It adapts existing DAGs to the target Airflow version, deploys them, and verifies them. Finally, the agent deploys the DAGs to cymbal-prod-af3 and confirms that they load without errors.

Data Agent Kit's migrations skill refactors the pipeline to Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling and verifies deployment in cymbal-prod-af3.

Two design choices remove the original problem:.

It has been revealed that scheduling moves into the watcher. PubsubPullTrigger is an event trigger, so an AssetWatcher can use it directly. The triggerer checks the subscription every 10 seconds in the background. Each batch of messages becomes an asset event that starts a run, with the messages in its payload. Nothing waits for the top of the hour, and no extra service has to call the Airflow REST API.

Industry observers note that each task processes one file rather than a full hour. Dynamic task mapping gives each new file its own task, and the subscription caps files at 128 MB. A busier hour means more tasks, not bigger ones.

Once the new DAG proves itself on live traffic, Amira pauses the hourly DAG in cymbal-prod.

Success! In a load test that replayed eight times normal peak traffic, clickstream_ingest simply ran more often. Memory per task didn't change.

Before: Airflow 2, hourly batch.

One clock hour: about 350 MB normally, 1.4 GB at campaign peak.

One file, a few MB each (at most 128 MB).

Grows with traffic: about 5 to 6 GB at campaign peak, well over 8 GB forecast for Black Friday.

Each agent works from the right vantage point. The console agent inspects production telemetry with your permissions and doesn't change anything, while the coding agent works in the IDE where code changes get reviewed, tested, and deployed.

Each step sets up the next one. The troubleshooting report offered a wider review, and each recommendation came with actionable advice. The upgrade check ended with next steps for the migrations skill, turning its report into the brief for the migration.

Agents propose and people decide. Amira scaled the workers, ran the infrastructure commands, and reviewed every change.

Sources indicate that static inspection estimates the work before live migration. Checking compatibility in the console scoped the effort in minutes, and the migration agent then made and verified the changes in a real environment.

Sources indicate that amira used the agents built into the console and her IDE. Two other capabilities didn't fit her story but are worth knowing about:.

You can bring your own agent with the Managed Airflow MCP server, now generally available, so any MCP-compatible agent can manage your environments, allowing you to list and trigger DAGs, check run status, and inspect failed task instances. Access is controlled through IAM, and read-only tools are flagged so you can limit agents to them.

It has been revealed that run agentic steps inside your pipelines with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider, which adds model-driven tasks that run side by side with deterministic ones in the same Airflow 3 DAG. Examples include LLM-based branching, agentic retries that tell a transient error from a bad input, and schema drift detection.

Explore Managed Airflow Agent troubleshooting and the overview of agentic capabilities.

Install Google Cloud Data Agent Kit using the documentation, the extension for VS Code, the plugin for coding agents (Antigravity, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI), or the open-source Airflow agent skills.

Learn about Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling.

Connect your agents to the Managed Airflow MCP server.

Build model-driven tasks and agents in DAGs with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider.

Special thanks to Jacek Iżykowski, Software Engineer on Managed Service for Apache Airflow, for authoring the original Cymbal Shops pipeline story and agent workflows featured in this post.

Note: As a fictional firm, any agent outputs from Cymbal Shops are shortened and illustrative, as are traffic and memory numbers.

Welcome RL Environments to the hub

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that reinforcement Learning environments give upcoming capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • According to recent reports, an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the upcoming RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that reinforcement Learning environments give upcoming capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

According to recent reports, an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the upcoming RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, owners of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

According to recent reports, the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

It has been revealed that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

In a recent development, framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer highlights the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

Industry observers note that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Industry observers note that here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

In a recent development, A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

According to recent reports, neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

Industry observers note that we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Industry observers note that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your consumers publish becomes visible to everyone else.

According to recent reports, if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.
  • By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff.
  • The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.

By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff.

The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

Sources indicate that as we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories.

1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:.

Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it.

According to recent reports, we tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

According to recent reports, 4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

According to recent reports, 5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

Performance Factory consists of a task service, dispatch loop, cloud execution, and subscriptions.

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

Each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

Sources indicate that A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

Once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

It has been revealed that the agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

Industry observers note that finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation, root caused, fix proposed, and resolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

The Regression Workflow’s steps include finding the root cause, proposing a fix, reviewing and deploying, and verifying recovery.

Finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The perf-forensics skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

Recent findings suggest that an alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

In a recent development, once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

It has been revealed that early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. If a rollout caused the slowdown, did similar requests that weren’t exposed stay healthy? If the suspected change was rolled back, did the affected metric recover?

Sources indicate that in one investigation, an agent traced failing ChatGPT conversations to errors in image downloads and marked the cause as found. The Codex reviewer noticed that the internal service responsible for locating files had already recovered while image requests were still failing. The diagnosis did not explain the continuing failures, so the AI reviewer reopened the investigation and recorded what still needed to be established.

We’ve had success breaking larger jobs into focused Codex turns. In a manual review of 100 root cause suggestions, we graded 70% as accurate, with 30% needing further refinement or not fully establishing causality. In the Regression Workflow, different turns investigate regressions, challenge diagnoses, and propose fixes to increase accuracy numbers through checks and balances.

In a recent development, once the diagnosis passes adversarial review, the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request. An engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it. We’ve put a significant amount of work into making this handoff as easy as possible. Each task has a report with an automatically generated summary of the regression, its impact, the root cause, and the proposed fix. We’ve tuned these summaries to be easy to scan, including metrics time series, CPU flame graphs, and traces to help engineers quickly understand the findings and inspect the evidence. Engineers can edit the PR directly or use the diagnosis to write their own fix. If they leave comments on the PR, the workflow wakes an agent to address them.

An example task report for a regression shows key details, root cause, and proposed fix.

Industry observers note that after an engineer deploys the fix, the workflow wakes an agent to check whether performance has returned to its earlier baseline. If it has, the agent marks the task as resolved. If performance has only partially recovered, the agent resolves the original regression and opens a latest task for the remaining slowdown, which may have a different cause. If there’s no improvement, the agent records what happened and sends the regression back for investigation.

In a recent development, getting fixes right has been harder than finding the cause. For example, we’ve seen cases where the agent-proposed changes are more complicated than necessary or introduce new issues. Similar to the root cause step, we added an adversarial review of each proposed fix to check whether they address the root cause and help catch bugs or unintended consequences. Some fixes also require higher level architectural decisions. For example, adding a cache might improve performance but introduce stale data. Changes like these benefit from guidance from an engineer who knows the service and can weigh the tradeoffs.

We’re building an evaluation and improvement loop using these cases. By comparing the fixes agents propose with the changes engineers ultimately merge, we can better understand where proposals fall short, build evals, and improve the workflow. We’re also working on using synthetic performance tests so agents can measure proposed fixes and revise them before asking an engineer for review. We’re also exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop.

Building and running the Performance Factory has taught us a lot about developing and operating agent workflows in production. Here are some lessons for teams building their own agentic workflows.

According to recent reports, the raw output from a Codex investigation can be a wall of text that’s hard to parse. It takes effort to figure out what the agent is claiming and track down the graphs to see whether the data backs it up. We want engineers to spend their attention on decisions rather than reconstructing the agent’s work.

In a recent development, agents can investigate more regressions than a team has time to read about. Our first version gave engineers a UI full of findings, but someone still had to decide which information mattered. One regression can also appear as several incidents across alerts, monitors, and channels. The workflow now links related incidents, groups them by the metrics teams care about, and ranks their estimated impact. Engineers can focus on adding context, weighing tradeoffs, and deciding what to ship.

Industry observers note that updating an investigation skill or upgrading the model can make the agent better at diagnosing some cases and worse at others, so we need to test their impact before updating them. We test two things separately: 1) how well the agent investigates and 2) how useful its summaries are to engineers.

In a recent development, for investigations, we backtest against past production incidents. We turn those incidents into a suite of test cases we can rerun when we change the skill. A Codex agent attempts to investigate and resolve the incident, and we compare the agent’s behavior to the actual past resolution data. Each case starts with a fresh Codex investigator and the original signal, stripped of details that might give away the answer.

Historical tests need care. Metrics and traces expire, while evidence collected after recovery can give away the cause. A test is only useful if we understand what evidence the investigator could see. The agent can inspect code and query production telemetry within set limits. It cannot use saved memories (notes from earlier investigations), read the incident writeup, or see results from previous runs. We also inspect its transcript afterward for information that might have spoiled the test.

Sources indicate that we score when the problem began, how large it was, and which requests were affected. We also evaluate how the agent uses evidence to rank possible causes and explain what remains uncertain. An agent can get the timing right and still blame the wrong deployment, so we score those separately.

According to recent reports, we evaluate task summaries using snapshots of saved tasks. These make particularly good backtests because summarization does not depend on external metrics or traces that expire. A separate grader checks whether an engineer unfamiliar with the system can understand what happened and why it matters, whether useful charts were kept, and whether the proposed next step is supported by the evidence.

Lastly, our agents need monitoring just as much as the services they investigate. A broken profiler or a missing permission can keep an agent from verifying what caused a slowdown. Those failures can be hard to spot in the final report, so we run an agent every day to look through messages and logs from recent runs for tool failures and access errors.

We use the Performance Factory to self-repair and fix the problems this check uncovers. When the same tool error blocks several investigations, the agent creates a task to fix it. If the cause is clear, an agent proposes a fix, and an engineer reviews the change and decides whether to merge it. After merging changes like this, we also use evals to check whether agents can get past the step that previously blocked them.

The Regression Workflow is just one instance of the agent factory pattern that moves tasks through explicit states. Agents advance the task when more work is ready; separate reviewers challenge the conclusions; engineers step in when the next decision requires judgment. Other workflows can reuse the same machinery with different states, instructions, and events.

From one workflow to many. The Performance Factory can coordinate agents across workflows, with agents in one workflow creating tasks for another.

In a recent development, right now, our Regression Workflow starts when an alert fires. However, we’re working on more proactive ways for the Performance Factory to find slowdowns and optimizations even when no alert fires. We want agents to use the large amount of fine-grained performance data we already collect to spot regressions our alerts miss or discover optimizations. By comparing different kinds of data (batches of CPU and memory profiles, heap dumps, and request traces across releases), an agent might notice a small increase in CPU for a given request. It can then open a task in the Regression Workflow to trace the increase to its cause, implement a fix, and open a PR for an engineer to review.

In cases where we already know what to look for, we’re working to encode known signals into more Performance Factory workflows. Our service rightsizing skill, for example, helps agents spot autoscaling settings that keep more replicas running than a service needs. When we learn to recognize a pattern like that, we want to build and regularly run a workflow for it across all our services, constantly optimizing in a rapidly changing environment. With the Performance Factory, what an engineer learns from one slowdown can shape how we investigate and fix the next one, even months later in a different service.

Next time you’re using ChatGPT and notice a slowdown, there’s a good chance the Performance Factory is already figuring out why. Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We’re already exploring whether agents can do this themselves. As product development keeps accelerating with Codex, performance systems need to become increasingly autonomous and self-improving to keep up. Codex already helps us build ChatGPT faster. Now it’s helping us keep ChatGPT fast.

Special thanks to the team that built the Performance Factory, as well as our post contributors Brendan Gregg, Pieter Hooimeijer, Nick Cooper, and Louis Brandy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AWS Partner Central Agents now help AWS Partners create and manage AWS Partner Central and AWS Marketplace support cases in one place.
  • Partners can handle a case from start to finish in one chat, with the full record in AWS Support Center.
  • The new support experience is available today to all AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers in the AWS Partner Central console and through the AWS Partner Central Agents MCP server.

Industry observers note that AWS Partner Central Agents now help AWS Partners create and manage AWS Partner Central and AWS Marketplace support cases in one place. The agents are available 24/7 and draw on Partner Central account details and authoritative, partner-specific knowledge from AWS to resolve most inquiries instantly. If a inquiry needs a support engineer, the agents will gather details and create a case. This reduces the time partners spend looking for help, and gives support teams the context they need to resolve cases faster.

Partners can handle a case from start to finish in one chat, with the full record in AWS Support Center. To create a case, partners can start describing their concern to AWS Partner Central Agents or use the prompt "get support." The agents gather additional details necessary to resolve the case, set the category, and draft the description. Partners review and submit the case, and the agents route the case to the right support team. In the same chat, partners can view case communications, track progress, post replies, and add attachments. With this launch, Partner Central and AWS Marketplace cases also move to AWS Support Center. There, partners can view the full case history and translate support correspondence into Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

The new support experience is available today to all AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers in the AWS Partner Central console and through the AWS Partner Central Agents MCP server. With the MCP server, partners can bring the support experience into tools such as Kiro, AWS Quick, CRM systems, and other AI clients. To learn more, see Getting support in AWS Partner Central, Getting support for AWS Marketplace, and Getting started with the Partner Central Agents MCP server.

Breaking: Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

According to recent reports, holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

It has been revealed that OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

Industry observers note that automationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Industry observers note that build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

Sources indicate that the tower is square in blueprint at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

In a recent development, no one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

Recent findings suggest that our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

According to recent reports, opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to latest foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

It has been revealed that these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

It has been revealed that both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most Gemini prototypes start the same way.
  • The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged.
  • For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Sources indicate that most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down.

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage firm, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

According to recent reports, in our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:.

It has been revealed that authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

Authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

Industry observers note that lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

Sources indicate that an AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the company, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

That is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:.

Industry observers note that A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Industry observers note that before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:.

Each person on the team runs one command:.

A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:.

Someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four reveals how.

That single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need new accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

In a recent development, gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:.

In a recent development, enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:.

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:.

Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

Sources indicate that openAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Industry observers note that your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

The good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:.

Industry observers note that keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

In a recent development, removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

It has been revealed that calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

According to recent reports, for people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:.

For the app, grant it to the service account:.

It takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:.

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:.

Sources indicate that if your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

In a recent development, the repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

To stop new keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

According to recent reports, some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:.

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:.

Live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:.

In a recent development, reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one fresh version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

It has been revealed that then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

Once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

According to recent reports, standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, upcoming requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

It has been revealed that you can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:.

Sources indicate that know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

Set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

According to recent reports, as soon as real users can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

According to recent reports, if your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:.

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.
