💡 Key Takeaways
  • Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.
  • We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research.
  • Industry observers note that one of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

Industry observers note that one of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.

Recent findings suggest that medChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:.

Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

Industry observers note that scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.

Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.

According to recent reports, property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how promptly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.

Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.

It has been revealed that small chemical changes can produce different property profiles. The task asks models to connect the structures with evidence about their behavior.

Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.

MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.

In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.

Recent findings suggest that these errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.

In a recent development, figure 1. The same input, different molecules.

These selected answers for compound 17 show a correct reconstruction, a smaller ring, and disconnected fragments.

While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.

We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.

It has been revealed that figure 2. Performance versus token usage.

Recent findings suggest that each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Tokens include reasoning and the final answer.

According to recent reports, the component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This reveals where models are strongest and where errors remain.

It has been revealed that figure 3. Component performance versus token usage.

Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.

In a recent development, where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.

Industry observers note that these results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Recent findings suggest that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Recent findings suggest that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

It has been revealed that this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

Sources indicate that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

Industry observers note that A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Sources indicate that those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a latest setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

Recent findings suggest that the most direct result is this: experts noted 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

According to recent reports, we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This reveals it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Recent findings suggest that blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

Recent findings suggest that as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

In a recent development, source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Recent findings suggest that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Industry observers note that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Recent findings suggest that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

According to recent reports, however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio.
  • Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions.
  • The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available.

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio. You can use it to compare foundation models side by side on throughput, latency, and cost, and then deploy or customize the model that fits your workload.

Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. The JumpStart leaderboard puts consistent measurements in one view. AWS evaluates every model on three reasoning benchmarks, MASSIVE-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro, using the same evaluation setup for each model. AWS also measures time to first token, throughput, and instance cost on SageMaker for each JumpStart deployment configuration. You can use all of the filters already available for JumpStart models, such as model provider, license, and input and output modality, to narrow the list. You can also choose a use case profile and an optimization goal (balanced, cost, latency, or throughput) to see the metrics for the configuration you initiative to deploy. At launch, the leaderboard covers more than 70 LLMs from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee.

The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available. To get started, open SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio and choose the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology and read the launch blog post.

#34175. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1385 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • According to recent reports, these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

According to recent reports, these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

Recent findings suggest that while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

In a recent development, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

In a recent development, numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an key gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

It has been revealed that you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

According to recent reports, the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is crucial for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

Industry observers note that we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Problems and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

Sources indicate that english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

It has been revealed that human feedback remains an notable part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as upcoming TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

  • Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested in Hebbia’s tests.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra.

Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested in Hebbia’s tests.

Percent of cited excerpts relevant to the question in Hebbia’s tests.

Percent of applicable presentation requirements met in Hebbia’s tests.

Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested on presentation requirements.

Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software manufacturer, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

“Traceability is really vital to our owners because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”.

Industry observers note that in Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely key. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita indicates.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

“I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita notes. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”.

GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

Industry observers note that “In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita notes.

In a recent development, in Hebbia, consumers can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Recent findings suggest that hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:.

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

Recent findings suggest that “Imagine getting an vital signal a few hours before your competitors,” she states. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our consumers.”.

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Amazon CloudWatch unveils telemetry filtering for the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, so you can stop paying to ingest telemetry you don't use.
  • In a recent development, you can now set cluster-wide include and exclude lists for namespaces, metric names, and pod and node labels.
  • Sources indicate that telemetry filtering is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics.

Today, Amazon CloudWatch unveils telemetry filtering for the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, so you can stop paying to ingest telemetry you don't use.

In a recent development, you can now set cluster-wide include and exclude lists for namespaces, metric names, and pod and node labels. Exclude the non-production namespaces you don't monitor, drop high-cardinality metrics by name, and keep only the labels you group by rather than every label on every resource. Because ingestion is billed per GB, collecting less lowers what you pay, and you can adjust filters with a single add-on configuration update as your clusters change.

Sources indicate that telemetry filtering is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry sent through the add-on is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing.

To get started, see Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.

#34170. Industry News: Combatting adversarial distillation

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2113 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Combatting adversarial distillation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
  • As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly notable role in how they can be used responsibly.
  • We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly notable role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Industry observers note that our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

Industry observers note that we’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

Recent findings suggest that the concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

Our models help owners with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to customers—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

Industry observers note that we started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1.

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

It has been revealed that we defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.

Sources indicate that adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

Industry observers note that we use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.

Industry observers note that tool-call coverage is notable because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.

With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As latest messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.

In a recent development, this work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.

Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

According to recent reports, to measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.

Sources indicate that we also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards.

GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards.

Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request.

Extracting protected reasoning from the current request.

Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

Recent findings suggest that we have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.

Recent findings suggest that in order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a upcoming window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.

We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.

Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:.

Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

It has been revealed that keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

It has been revealed that we have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum⁠(opens in a upcoming window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.

As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

In a recent development, related work from Anthropic⁠(opens in a fresh window) reported a similar advantage when training on full reasoning transcripts rather than summaries on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering benchmark. Our result highlights this advantage extends to frontier cybersecurity.

AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • According to recent reports, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

According to recent reports, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates upcoming tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

In a recent development, consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Recent findings suggest that soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

In a recent development, these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

In a recent development, autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into upcoming executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

Recent findings suggest that autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

Recent findings suggest that we distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

Industry observers note that the generator creates upcoming tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

In a recent development, the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a fresh target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

According to recent reports, the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

It has been revealed that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Sources indicate that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Industry observers note that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Sources indicate that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Industry observers note that failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

In a recent development, passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

Recent findings suggest that A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

Sources indicate that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

According to recent reports, after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We proposal to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

In a recent development, we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

Sources indicate that the synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

Industry observers note that we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates fresh tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

Latest Update: AWS Private CA now supports X.509 IAM condition keys

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (311 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued.
  • Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains.
  • Industry observers note that you can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).

In a recent development, AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued. You can write IAM policies that allow or deny a certificate request based on its subject, subject alternative names (SANs), public key, signature algorithm, validity period, key usage, extended key usage, and basic constraints. You can share one private CA across teams and accounts, and each team can issue only the certificates your policies allow.

Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains. To keep each team to its own domain names, customers ran a separate CA for each team or built their own authorization layer in front of AWS Private CA. Now, AWS Private CA evaluates your policies against the certificate as it would be issued, before anything is signed, and denies requests that don't comply. For example, you can limit each account to DNS names in its own subdomain, cap certificate lifetimes, require specified key algorithms and key sizes across your organization, and reserve CA certificates for your PKI team.

Industry observers note that you can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Each key takes its value from the final certificate, whether the attribute comes from the certificate signing request (CSR), the certificate template, or API passthrough, so moving an attribute to a different input doesn't get it past a policy.

Industry observers note that X.509 IAM condition keys are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where AWS Private CA is available. AWS Private CA charges still apply. To get started, see X.509 certificate condition keys in the AWS Private CA User Guide.

#34167. Perplexity and Intelligence
