📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that torchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

Sources indicate that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a latest backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

It has been revealed that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

It has been revealed that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron consumers use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

In a recent development, now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Recent findings suggest that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

In a recent development, nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

Recent findings suggest that the command below rolls out training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Industry observers note that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, consumers can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support.

Recent findings suggest that today, we are proud to announce that Gartner has recognized Google as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM). According to recent reports, today's threat landscape requires a newly introduced approach to security operations that can keep pace with the speed, scale, and sophistication of autonomous attacks. Traditional SIEM architectures centralized logs and alerts, but left analysts to manually stitch together context, write and maintain detections, and craft response playbooks.

Now, working alongside analysts, autonomous agents can reason over enterprise context and use frontline threat intelligence to compress detection and response cycles from days to seconds.

We feel our placement in the 2026 Leaders Quadrant reflects our rapid pace of engineering innovation in Google Security Operations. Since last year’s Magic Quadrant report, we’ve focused on turning the agentic SOC from vision into daily reality for our customers, helping security teams scale their expertise and outpace attackers. We expanded Gemini in Security Operations from a helpful assistant into a team of purpose-built agents, including the Triage and Investigation agent, Threat Hunt agent, Detection Engineering agent, and Third-party Context agent. We also introduced agentic automation to orchestrate automated actions in playbooks with agents.

Security teams are also able to assess their exposure to breaking threats, ranging from the Emerging Threats Centers to Mandiant rule packs and other curated detections, hunt and analyze threats faster using familiar syntax with GoogleSQL in Search, and run simplified operation at scale through native Data Processing Pipelines, the Health Hub, and a unified investigation and case management experience.

The shift to an agentic SOC with Google Security Operations is already delivering quantifiable time savings and operational relief for defenders. “Since implementing Google SecOps, we’ve cut false positives by 42%—exceeding all our expectations. Our analysts no longer spend their days validating noise on glass. Instead, they’re focused on solving complex problems and building proactive protections across our 100-year-old enterprise,” said David Nagel, global CISO, Genuine Parts Organization.

Traditional detection engineering — which requires reverse-engineering attacks, manually authoring rules and validating coverage before pushing to production — requires intense resourcing from busy security teams. Our Detection Engineering agent transforms this workflow by automating rule creation and simulating threat coverage on demand. This can enable organizations to compress the entire end-to-end testing and deployment lifecycle down to under 30 minutes.

In addition to streamlining detection engineering, Google Security Operations brings agentic capabilities to threat hunting. Deep threat hunting across months of historical telemetry has historically been a manual, labor-intensive process restricted to specialized hunt teams or senior analysts, often demanding up to a full day of dedicated effort per hunt.

The Threat Hunting agent uplevels the SOC by autonomously generating and executing comprehensive hunt prepares directly from threat intelligence to uncover advanced adversaries and emerging tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), helping customers complete in less than an hour what previously took a full day.

According to recent reports, “With threats doubling every year, we have to fight machines with machines. Google SecOps and Gemini give our junior analysts 'superpowers' to act like senior threat hunters, cutting our response times from hours to minutes so LATAM flights stay on time and our passengers safe,” mentioned André Pires Ferreira Magalhães, CISO, LATAM Airlines.

Industry observers note that according to a new Business Value report from IDC, security operations teams using Gemini in Security Operations have achieved a 98% faster mean time to identify threats, a 50% reduction in impactful security incidents per month, and an 84% reduction in the time spent manually drafting security reports and incident summaries. Ultimately, these efficiency gains allow organizations to scale their defenses and redirect their most experienced, time-limited talent toward strategic security priorities.

Furthermore, those organizations saw a 319% three-year ROI and a 7-month payback, $5.4M average annual benefits per organization and 38.2% team efficiency gain from using Gemini in production.

Sources indicate that recognition in the Gartner Magic Quadrant is ultimately a reflection of the security teams who rely on Google Security Operations every day and push us to set new standards. Your real-world feedback and hard-won operational insights help us turn cutting-edge technology into a true defender’s advantage.

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

Sources indicate that FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

It has been revealed that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each fresh token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

According to recent reports, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Sources indicate that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Sources indicate that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them newly introduced paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

In a recent development, several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Industry observers note that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Recent findings suggest that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

In a recent development, scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system⁠(opens in a new window) since the first ones were revealed in 1992⁠(opens in a new window).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.

Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system⁠(opens in a new window) since the first ones were revealed in 1992⁠(opens in a new window). A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.

It has been revealed that *Data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table⁠(opens in a new window). 2026 data are year to date through November 24, 2026.

It has been revealed that astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope⁠(opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90⁠(opens in a new window).

Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.

Sources indicate that both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.

One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit reveals up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.

Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged.

It has been revealed that bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for.

Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.

These four curves show the same Kepler observations aligned on a 13.77-day cycle.

Recent findings suggest that the second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years.

Industry observers note that byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.

Recent findings suggest that byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives.

Kepler watched one field for four years. TESS surveyed both hemispheres in its first 26 sectors, from 2018 to 2020. The star field comes from NASA’s TESS mosaic through September 2025⁠(opens in a fresh window), clipped to that original survey footprint. The wider gap reveals where TESS pointed farther north during six observing sectors. The inset marks KIC 5689121⁠(opens in a new window) in the original Kepler field⁠(opens in a new window). See NASA’s final prime-mission coverage maps⁠(opens in a new window) and its earlier field-of-view animation⁠(opens in a new window).

The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running.

When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.

Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, shows up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence.

Recent findings suggest that for Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a question that can be tested. If a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing. Further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected, while additional checks can help determine what is causing it.

It has been revealed that you can contribute without owning a telescope. NASA’s Exoplanet Watch⁠(opens in a new window) lets you request data and learn to plot a light curve yourself. Its broader exoplanet citizen science programs⁠(opens in a new window) offer other ways to participate.

It has been revealed that if you have access to a telescope, Exoplanet Watch walks customers through how to collect data on transiting exoplanets and participate in observation campaigns. AAVSO’s Exoplanet Observing Program⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) can show you how to measure a dip in starlight and share your observations with the researchers studying that planet. And the Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets⁠(opens in a new window) coordinates volunteers around the world with a certain type of telescope to observe the same star, helping astronomers catch transits that can last longer than a single night.

Astronomy has a long history of people around the world following their curiosity and sharing what they find. Bond and Byrd are part of that tradition. Their searches are still open, but they turned a love of the night sky into leads that other astronomers can investigate. We want more people to have that opportunity, in astronomy and across science.

If you want to follow along with new findings, practical guidance, and perspectives from researchers using AI to advance science check out the OpenAI science blog⁠.

You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

According to recent reports, AWS Partners can now map their target accounts against AWS records and find where to collaborate with AWS on joint go-to-market before an opportunity exists. Account Mapping and Planning in AWS Partner Central replaces manual, spreadsheet-based account mapping. Upload a target account list through CSV, API, or CRM integration, and accounts are matched automatically against AWS records, including accounts without an ACE opportunity and in any country.

It has been revealed that partners can use Account Mapping and Planning to enrich matched accounts with AWS Marketplace propensity insights, solution-level purchase likelihood, and eligibility for programs such as the Partner Greenfield Program and the Partner-Led Sales Motion. This helps Partners prioritize high-propensity and program-eligible accounts for go-to-market activity. Eligible Partners can also request joint account planning with AWS sales on accounts marked Qualified, so AWS and Partner teams can align on an account strategy earlier. Account planning is available to Consulting Partners that are ACE-eligible, Premier tier and managed by an AWS Partner Development Manager (PDM), and to ISVs that are ACE-eligible, enrolled in the SaaS Co-sell Benefit program and PDM-managed.

It has been revealed that account Mapping and Planning is available under the Sell tab in AWS Partner Central, and account matching and enrichment are open to all ACE-eligible Partners. Partners can work in the Partner Central console, through the API and SDK, through the Partner Central MCP server, or through an integration Partner to connect results to their CRM.

To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central, go to the Account Mapping page under the Sell tab, and upload a target account list.

AI governance becomes a must-have for compliance in 2027

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, artificial intelligence in financial services compliance is leaving the experimental phase behind.
  • Experts at RegTech firm Saifr have identified five trends that are already shaping technology budgets, operating models and supervisory expectations.
  • In a recent development, the first is the move from standalone tools to embedded intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, artificial intelligence in financial services compliance is leaving the experimental phase behind. As 2027 approaches, firms are no longer asking whether AI works. They are asking how to build it into daily workflows and decision-making without losing the governance and transparency regulators demand.

Experts at RegTech firm Saifr have identified five trends that are already shaping technology budgets, operating models and supervisory expectations.

In a recent development, the first is the move from standalone tools to embedded intelligence. Most firms right now apply AI to discrete tasks such as marketing reviews, KYC investigations or communications surveillance.

It has been revealed that that is changing as organisations judge AI by outcomes, such as spotting risks earlier or cutting unnecessary manual review. Saifr regulatory and compliance advisor Jim McCarthy said, “We’re moving from AI as a tool to AI as an embedded component of compliance operations.” Contextual AI that interprets intent, regulatory intelligence that explains its reasoning and workflow-integrated systems are driving the change.

According to recent reports, context is the second differentiator. General-purpose assistants are useful for research, but compliance work demands an understanding of specific business and regulatory settings. Saifr V.P. and U.S. head of data science Last Feremenga remarked, “Organizations are evaluating solutions not by the volume of alerts that they’re producing, but by how much context each of the alerts has.” Firms increasingly want tools that explain why an problem matters and what should happen next.

Third, AI governance is shifting from best practice to business necessity. Regulators are not carving out separate rules for AI. Instead, they are folding it into existing obligations, leaving firms accountable for outcomes whether a person or a machine made the call.

Saifr V.P. and head of compliance Allison Lagosh said, “You need to have a good inventory of your AI systems. Know how you’re using AI to support your business and what program you have in place to oversee it.” Clear inventories, defined oversight, human review, vendor governance and documentation are becoming essential, particularly as firms navigate a patchwork of state, federal and international rules, including the EU AI Act.

Sources indicate that the fourth trend is signal intelligence. In AML, financial crime and due diligence, the problem is no longer access to data but knowing which signals demand action. Recent enforcement cases show that warning signs often existed but went unaddressed. Leaders that build signal-rich ecosystems will spot threats faster and reduce blind spots.

Finally, purpose-built models are outperforming larger rivals on specialised work. Saifr founder and CEO Vall Herard mentioned, “You don’t need your marketing review model to be able to compose a song. You just need it to be very good at what it’s supposed to do.” Smaller, task-specific models often offer advantages in cost, explainability and governance, encouraging architectures built from multiple specialised models.

The message is clear, in that AI in compliance is becoming operational. The winners will be those that pair innovation with strong governance and human oversight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this latest generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Recent findings suggest that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

In a recent development, API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

In a recent development, community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

It has been revealed that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. Reversa, a Madrid-based RegTech firm developing artificial intelligence agents to handle regulatory tasks for businesses and public bodies, has secured €750,000 in fresh capital, which includes a pre-seed round headed by Itnig.

Itnig, the investment vehicle of the founders of Factorial, led the pre-seed portion of the raise. The Jobandtalent co-founders also joined, as did angel investors drawn from the legal and technology industries, among them executives at HappyRobot, Fuse Energy and several multinational banking and energy groups. Reversa also receives backing from Enisa and from the Neotec programme run by CDTI.

Sources indicate that the latest capital will help Reversa widen the international reach of its regulatory infrastructure and develop sector-focused products on top of it, targeting areas including financial services, energy and real estate. On the urban planning side, the firm is developing agents designed to streamline land-use permits, a recognised obstacle to building new homes. Hiring across engineering, product and sales is also planned.

In a recent development, reversa’s platform features a regulatory radar, through which agents link directly to official sources, assess how each regulatory change affects a business and support the steps needed to put it into practice. The technology also tackles operational and commercial challenges, such as pinpointing which legal framework applies when a company enters a newly introduced market, or automating compliance checks on a new product.

Industry observers note that customers also use it for jurisdiction-specific legal research and for drafting and revising contracts and policies. For public affairs teams, the agents track legislative procedures in real time, helping organisations prepare for upcoming rule changes and engage with the lawmaking process.

The company points to the scale of the compliance burden facing organisations worldwide. Citing PwC’s global CEO survey, it notes that business leaders consider the regulatory environment one of the biggest obstacles to transformation. According to TheCityUK and PwC, compliance now accounts for over 13% of operating costs in UK financial services. A National Association of Manufacturers study puts the annual cost of US federal regulation at $3.08 trillion, or 12% of GDP, with smaller firms hit hardest. DLA Piper figures show European regulators imposed roughly €1.2bn in data protection fines in 2025.

Regulation also slows major projects. The European Parliamentary Research Service reports that EU electricity transmission projects can take up to a decade, with permitting consuming over half of that time. In housing, securing a building permit takes between three and 24 months depending on the country, while the European Commission estimates the EU needs an extra 650,000 homes annually. The Bank of Spain calculates that Spain alone faces a shortfall of about 750,000.

Sources indicate that founded in 2025 by Tomás Burgaleta Alonso, Iñigo Martín Llorente and Santiago Aliaga Estella, Reversa organises each jurisdiction’s rules using official sources and automates regulatory monitoring, legal research, compliance and public affairs on that foundation. It describes this category as regulatory superintelligence.

Reversa co-founder and CEO Iñigo Martín Llorente said, “Reversa solves regulatory problems for large companies and public institutions. To do so, it structures the regulation of each jurisdiction from its official sources, keeps it up to date and, on top of that infrastructure, builds specific solutions with artificial intelligence agents for different use cases.”.

Reversa co-founder and CTO Santiago Aliaga Estella mentioned, “Reversa is a regulatory system of action. It does not just capture information; it delivers the finished work. We build a digital replica of each jurisdiction, with its laws, institutions and procedures, and on top of it we automate workflows with agents that resolve our customers’ tasks end to end.”.

Lending will be unified on a single base, with clients routed through automated, guided or bespoke journeys depending on how complex their requirements are.

Recent findings suggest that rabobank anticipates that a large share of its clients will use the automated route, which should allow relationship managers to devote more time to supporting customers’ growth. nCino’s built-in AI and governance tools are expected to let the bank expand its use of AI across the whole lending process in a responsible way, with staff retaining authority over decisions and with transparency, auditability and oversight embedded throughout.

Industry observers note that nCino serves more than 2,700 customers globally, ranging from community banks, credit unions and independent mortgage banks to some of the world’s biggest financial institutions. Its agentic platform is built specifically for financial services and other regulated sectors, pairing AI agents with human teams in a “dual workforce” model intended to remove inefficiencies, improve decision-making and produce better results for end customers.

#34116. GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4187 w)

GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our GPT‑6 family of models can design latest protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
  • In a recent development, an internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks.
  • In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design latest protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

In a recent development, an internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Industry observers note that proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

In a recent development, using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

In a recent development, we ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

It has been revealed that the models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

In a recent development, the model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

Industry observers note that with our research partner, Onava⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein highlighted evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

Sources indicate that our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

In a recent development, we gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.

We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study⁠(opens in a new window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

Industry observers note that an internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.

According to recent reports, we tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose upcoming ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

According to recent reports, for three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

Sources indicate that we also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.

Industry observers note that given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both indicated signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.

According to recent reports, the unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

Industry observers note that researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design newly introduced loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.

Recent findings suggest that we started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design newly introduced sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.

We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

According to recent reports, A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.

Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.

Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a upcoming enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.

We tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench⁠(opens in a upcoming window), including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding.

Sources indicate that for each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold⁠(opens in a new window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.

In a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.

An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.

In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH⁠(opens in a new window), a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.

Many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.

It has been revealed that we counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.

An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.

Many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.

For our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset⁠(opens in a upcoming window), a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.

In practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt. We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset⁠(opens in a new window), where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions⁠(opens in a new window), and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock⁠(opens in a new window) reached 60%.

It has been revealed that an internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple reveals the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.

Where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we demonstrated the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.

With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.

Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.

Each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray indicates the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.

We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.

We drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.

Sources indicate that in one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.

In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.

Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.

The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.

What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.

Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments.

Each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.

Industry observers note that it is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.

Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.

According to recent reports, some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.

Sources indicate that the laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.

It has been revealed that this work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

Sources indicate that find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.

Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

Design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.

As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for latest medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework⁠ guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.

While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • According to recent reports, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • It has been revealed that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

According to recent reports, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

It has been revealed that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

Recent findings suggest that the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a latest backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

It has been revealed that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

In a recent development, TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

In a recent development, models too major for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

It has been revealed that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Sources indicate that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

According to recent reports, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Industry observers note that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It has been revealed that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel looks. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Sources indicate that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Industry observers note that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

Lassie, the Swedish pet health and insurance business, has struck a deal with MoneySuperMarket that makes the comparison platform the sole UK site where consumers can compare and purchase its prevention-focused pet cover for an initial three months.

The arrangement is designed to widen Lassie’s reach among UK pet owners. Through its app, policyholders can make a claim simply by taking a photo of their vet’s receipt, with the firm’s AI-driven process seeing upwards of 60% of claims worldwide wrapped up in roughly six minutes end to end. The same app also lets customers handle the day-to-day management of their policy.

Lassie entered the UK market in July and pairs insurance with tailored preventative care, aiming to support healthier pets through routine activities. Consumers receive weekly programmes shaped around their animal’s breed, age and life stage, covering areas such as nutrition, vaccinations, socialisation and training. The platform offers over 200 short courses alongside expert video content, and owners collect points for finishing health-related tasks. These points can then be converted into cheaper premiums, discounts and loyalty perks.

The InsurTech counts the owners of over 300,000 cats and dogs as customers across the UK, Sweden, Germany and France.

Recent findings suggest that moneySuperMarket director of insurance Sara Newell stated, “We’re always looking for newly introduced ways to give our customers more choice and help them find pet insurance that works for them. Lassie brings something genuinely different to the market by combining cover with practical tools and rewards that help owners look after their pets. We’re pleased to make Lassie available through a UK price comparison site for the first time, making it easier for pet owners to compare their options and find the right cover.”.

It has been revealed that lassie CEO and co-founder Hedda Båverud Olsson mentioned, “Partnering with MoneySuperMarket puts Lassie in front of a far larger share of UK pet owners at the moment they’re looking for cover. We know that many pet health problems can be prevented, so we believe pet insurance should do more than pay claims once something has gone wrong. We built Lassie to help owners stay ahead of issues, using AI, behavioural science and gamification to make everyday pet care simpler and more rewarding. We’re delighted to bring this approach to MoneySuperMarket’s customers, helping them keep their pets healthier for longer and making it simple to claim when they need to.”.
